# KV Cache: Enabling Efficient Long-Context Inference

## What Is KV Cache?

In transformer-based language models, inference proceeds autoregressively—generating one token at a time, with each new token depending on all previous tokens. During this process, the model computes attention between the current token and every preceding token in the sequence. For each attention operation, the model projects input embeddings into three vectors: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V). The attention scores are calculated as softmax(Q · K^T) applied to V.

KV cache refers to storing the computed Key and Value tensors from previously processed tokens so they don't need to be recomputed when generating subsequent tokens. Instead of recalculating K and V for positions 1 through t−1 every time we generate token t, we cache these tensors in GPU memory and retrieve them directly. Only the Q vector for the new token must be computed fresh.

## Why It Matters for Long Context

Without KV caching, generating a sequence of N tokens requires O(N²) Key and Value computations—each generation step repeats work from all prior steps. With KV caching, this drops to O(N): we compute K and V once per position, then reuse them for all future generations. This transformation makes autoregressive generation computationally tractable.

As context length grows, the quadratic savings become substantial. A 128k context window would require roughly 8 billion K/V computations without caching; with caching, only 128k computations are needed. # KV Cache: Enabling Efficient Long-Context Inference

## What Is KV Cache?

KV cache is an inference optimization technique that stores the key-value tensors from attention computations across generation steps, avoiding redundant calculations during autoregressive token generation.

During each forward pass through a transformer, the attention mechanism computes query, key, and value projections for all tokens in the context. When generating new tokens autoregressively, only the current token's query vector is needed—yet standard implementation recomputes keys and values for *all* previous tokens at every step. KV cache eliminates this waste by caching the computed keys and values after their initial creation, allowing subsequent steps to retrieve them directly from memory rather than recalculating them.

## Why It Matters for Long Context

As context length grows, the computational savings from KV caching become substantial. For a sequence of length *n*, naive autoregressive generation requires O(n²) operations across all steps, while KV caching reduces this to O(n). Beyond raw performance, KV caching addresses three critical challenges in long-context scenarios.

Memory bandwidth becomes the primary bottleneck when processing thousands of tokens per request. Recomputing keys and values for a 128k-token context at every decoding step would require reading massive weight matrices repeatedly; caching these intermediate results trades computation for strategic memory access, dramatically improving throughput.

Latency also improves significantly because each generation step performs only the minimal necessary computation—the new token's query projection plus attention over cached keys and values—rather than reprocessing the entire context.
